value.description_seasoned: Field corn (Zea mays var. indentata), or dent corn, is a tall, frost-tender warm-season grass grown to full maturity for its hard, starchy grain rather than picked green like sweet corn. The ears dry down on the stalk to a hard, dented kernel, then are shelled and ground into cornmeal, grits, hominy, or masa, or kept as livestock and poultry feed. Representative types run from towering open-pollinated heirlooms (John Haulk, Cocke's Prolific, Reid's Yellow Dent, Bloody Butcher) to compact modern grain hybrids chosen by relative maturity. It is wind-pollinated and block-planted, a heavy nitrogen feeder with the same critical moisture window at tasseling and silking as sweet corn. The one isolation rule that matters: dent pollen crossing into sweet corn turns the kernels starchy, and crossing into popcorn destroys its pop, so isolate by about 300 feet or stagger tasseling by roughly two weeks.
value.description_beginner: Field corn, also called dent corn, is a tall grass grown not for fresh eating but for the hard, dry grain inside the ear. You let the ears ripen and dry right on the stalk, then shell off the kernels to grind into cornmeal, grits, or masa for tortillas, or to feed to livestock and poultry. Old open-pollinated types like John Haulk and Cocke's Prolific can tower up to 15 feet, while modern grain hybrids are shorter and faster. Like all corn it is pollinated by wind, so you plant it in a square block of short rows, not a single line, so the tassels can dust the silks and fill the ears. One important warning: field corn pollen will drift into nearby sweet corn or popcorn and ruin them, turning sweet kernels starchy and keeping popcorn from popping, so keep them at least 300 feet apart or time your plantings so they tassel about two weeks apart.
value.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest at full physiological maturity and beyond, when the husks are brown and papery, the kernels are hard and fully dented, and a black layer has formed at the kernel base (about 30 to 35 percent kernel moisture at that point). For storage the grain needs to reach roughly 13 to 15 percent moisture, so leave sound ears to field-dry on the stalk in dry weather, or pick at hard dent and finish drying them under cover. There is no narrow window as with milk-stage sweet corn.
value.harvest_ready_beginner: Field corn is ready to harvest when the whole ear has dried down on the stalk: the husks have turned brown and papery, the silks are long dead, and the kernels are hard and dented, not soft or milky. Press a thumbnail into a kernel and it should barely dent. Unlike sweet corn there is no rush, so in good weather you can leave the ears to dry further on the plant. Then pick them, pull back the husks, and finish drying them indoors before you shell off the kernels.
value.soil_prep_seasoned: Work compost or aged manure into a full-sun bed before planting; corn is a heavy feeder and roots deeply. Lay the planting out as a BLOCK of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid beats one long row) so wind pollination fills the ears evenly. Keep field corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, since its dent pollen crosses into them and ruins them, turning sweet corn starchy and keeping popcorn from popping.
value.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a sunny spot and mix in compost before planting, because corn is a hungry crop that grows tall. Plant it in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row: a small square (say four rows of four plants) lets the wind carry pollen from the tassels onto the silks, so the ears fill out with full kernels instead of gappy ones. Keep field corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, because its pollen will drift in and spoil them.

value.name: Popcorn

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam suits corn best. Its roots run deep and it feeds heavily, so a soil rich in organic matter that holds moisture through the tasseling and silking window without waterlogging gives the fullest ears.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Corn grows best in deep, rich, well-drained soil like loam. Because it grows tall and feeds heavily, mixing in compost before planting helps the soil hold the steady moisture the plants need when the ears are forming.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both grow good corn if drainage is sound. Sandy beds warm faster and suit early sowings but dry out and leach nitrogen quicker, so they need more frequent water and sidedressing; heavier soils hold feeding longer but must be worked so they do not crust over the seed.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils can grow corn as long as they drain well. Sandy soil warms up early but dries out and loses fertilizer faster, so water and feed a little more often. Heavier soil holds food longer but should be loosened so it does not form a hard crust over the seeds.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid cold, wet, poorly drained ground. Corn seed rots or suffers chilling injury when sown into soil below 60°F, and standing water stunts the shallow feeder roots and starves the plant of the nitrogen it needs.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Stay away from cold, soggy, poorly drained soil. Corn seed sits and rots in cold, wet ground instead of sprouting, and standing water keeps the roots from feeding, which corn needs to do a lot of.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Corn likes deep, rich, well-drained soil. If water pools on your bed after rain, work in compost and consider a raised bed so the roots never sit wet.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam with compost worked in before planting. The load-bearing traits are warmth at sowing and steady moisture with high fertility through tasseling and silking.

ph.note_beginner: Corn does best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around a pH of 6.0 to 6.8. Most garden beds are already close; a soil test is the only way to know for sure and to catch soil that is too acidic.
ph.note_seasoned: A soil pH of 6.0 to 6.8 suits popcorn. Lime an acidic bed to reach that range the season before, and confirm both pH and fertility with a soil test, since corn's heavy feeding rewards a well-limed, well-fed bed.

fertilizer.timing: starter at planting; sidedress at knee-high and again at tasseling
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder. Work a balanced starter into the bed at planting, then sidedress nitrogen twice: once when plants are knee-high and again as the tassels form, the two windows when demand peaks. Sandy soils and heavy rain leach nitrogen, so split the sidedressing further where that applies.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Corn is hungry, especially for nitrogen. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil at planting, then feed again when the plants are about knee-high and once more when the tassels appear at the top. Those are the times corn needs the most food. In sandy soil or after heavy rain, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen now: your corn is at the knee-high stage where demand climbs steeply.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your corn. It is about knee-high now, which is when it needs a nitrogen boost.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Nitrogen-forward feeding: a balanced starter, then nitrogen sidedressings at knee-high and tasseling.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Corn wants plenty of nitrogen. Use a balanced fertilizer at planting, then feed nitrogen again as it grows.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Follow the label rate for a heavy-feeding vegetable; a common approach is a balanced starter plus two nitrogen sidedressings.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Use the amount on the fertilizer label for a hungry vegetable, then two lighter nitrogen feedings as it grows.

companions.note_beginner: Corn is the tall centerpiece of the classic Three Sisters planting with beans and squash. The beans feed the soil the corn is so hungry for, and the squash shades the ground below. Keep corn away from tomatoes, since the two share the same ear-and-fruit worm.
companions.note_seasoned: Corn anchors the traditional Three Sisters trio: beans climb it and fix nitrogen for its heavy demand, and squash sprawls below as a living mulch. The main caution is tomatoes, which share the pest Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm / tomato fruitworm), so a shared planting can concentrate it.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The Three Sisters partner: beans pull nitrogen from the air and enrich the soil for hungry corn, and can climb the stalks.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters is the best-documented historical polyculture; the corn-bean nitrogen relationship is sound and traditional, not a crop-specific measured trial. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pole beans use the cornstalk as a living trellis and fix nitrogen that offsets corn's heavy demand; the pairing is the well-documented Three Sisters polyculture. The benefit is soil-and-structure rather than a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The third Sister: its big sprawling leaves shade the soil around the corn, holding moisture and smothering weeds.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters ground-cover role is well established and structural; foliage-diversity pest disruption is plausible but not corn-specific measured. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Squash rounds out the trio as a ground-covering living mulch that shades soil, conserves moisture, and suppresses weeds around the corn. A soil-and-space benefit; give it room so it does not swamp young corn.

good_seasoned.name: Beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The Three Sisters partner; beans fix nitrogen that helps carry corn's heavy feeding demand, and climb the stalks.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters, documented traditional Native American polyculture.

good_seasoned.name: Squash
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third Sister; its sprawling canopy shades soil and suppresses weeds around the upright corn.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are hit by the same worm, called the corn earworm on corn and the tomato fruitworm on tomatoes, so growing them together can build it up.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Corn earworm and tomato fruitworm are the same species, Helicoverpa zea; a shared host planting concentrates it. Sound, consistently reported mechanism; no opened controlled trial quantifying the garden effect this session. mechanistic/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn and tomato share Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm on corn, tomato fruitworm on tomato). Interplanting gives the pest two sequential hosts in one spot, so separating them limits the buildup.

bad_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn and tomato share the pest Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm / tomato fruitworm); a shared planting concentrates it.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared Helicoverpa zea host; mechanism sound and consistently reported.

pests.name: Corn earworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Chewed, frass-fouled kernels at the ear tip where a fat, striped caterpillar has fed under the husk; silks may be clipped, and tip damage opens the door to mold.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fat, striped caterpillar tunneling into the tip of the ear under the husk, leaving chewed kernels and dark droppings. It usually stays near the tip, but the damage can let mold in.
pests.cause_seasoned: The corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea), whose moths lay eggs on fresh silks; the hatching larvae follow the silks down into the ear tip. It is the same species as the tomato fruitworm.
pests.cause_beginner: The corn earworm, a caterpillar whose moth lays eggs on the silks. The young caterpillars crawl down the silks into the ear. It is the same pest as the tomato fruitworm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Because most feeding is confined to the ear tip, the loss is often cosmetic: cut off the damaged tip at the kitchen. A few drops of mineral oil applied to the silk channel after pollination is a traditional home tactic; a spinosad or Bt product timed to fresh silks is the labeled organic option.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The good news is the worm usually stays at the very tip, so you can just cut that part off. A classic trick is a few drops of vegetable or mineral oil on the silks after they have been pollinated, and an organic spray such as Bt or spinosad works if you time it to fresh silks.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Choose varieties with tight, long husk cover, which slows the larvae, and plant early so the crop silks before peak moth flights in late summer.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick varieties with long, tight husks that make it harder for the worm to get in, and plant early so the ears silk before the moths are at their worst in late summer.

pests.name: European corn borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small shot-hole feeding in the whorl leaves, then sawdust-like frass at leaf axils and pin-sized entry holes in the stalk and ear shank; tunneled stalks weaken and can snap.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny holes in the young leaves, then sawdust-like droppings where the leaves meet the stalk, and small holes bored into the stalk itself. Badly tunneled stalks can break.
pests.cause_seasoned: The European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis), a caterpillar that first feeds in the leaf whorl, then bores into stalks and ear shanks, weakening the plant from inside.
pests.cause_beginner: The European corn borer, a caterpillar that starts by chewing the young leaves, then tunnels into the stalks, hollowing them out.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scout the whorls and pick off egg masses and young larvae before they bore in; a Bt product reaches them only while they are still feeding in the open whorl. Once inside the stalk they are protected.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Check the young leaf whorls and rub out the egg patches and small caterpillars before they tunnel in. An organic Bt spray only works while they are still out on the leaves; once inside the stalk you cannot reach them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Shred and turn under cornstalks after harvest, since the borer overwinters in old stalks; rotating away from last year's patch helps too.
pests.prevention_beginner: Chop up and dig in the old cornstalks after harvest, because the borer spends the winter inside them, and move your corn to a new spot each year.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Young seedlings clipped off at or just above the soil line overnight, often toppled and left; a gray, greasy-looking caterpillar curls up just below the surface nearby.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Young corn plants cut off right at the ground overnight, as if with scissors. If you dig near a cut plant, you often find a fat gray caterpillar curled up in the soil.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cutworms, the soil-dwelling larvae of several night-flying moths, which sever tender seedling stems at the base as they feed after dark.
pests.cause_beginner: Cutworms, fat caterpillars that live in the soil and come out at night to chew through young stems at the base.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick at night or just under the soil around fresh damage; a cardboard or foil collar pushed an inch into the soil around each seedling blocks them.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Go out at night with a flashlight and pick them off, or dig around a freshly cut plant to find the culprit. A little collar of cardboard or foil pushed into the soil around each stem keeps them out.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the bed weed-free before planting, since cutworm moths lay in weedy ground, and delay sowing until the soil is warm and seedlings grow fast through the vulnerable stage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear weeds from the bed before you plant, because the moths lay their eggs in weedy soil, and plant into warm soil so the seedlings grow quickly past the tender stage.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed, leaving fine pinholes and shot-hole pitting in the leaves of young plants; heavy early feeding stunts seedlings and can transmit Stewart's wilt.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny dark beetles that hop away when you get close, leaving the young leaves peppered with little pinholes. Bad early damage stunts small plants and can spread a corn disease.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species that feed on corn seedlings; the corn flea beetle also carries the bacterium that causes Stewart's wilt from plant to plant.
pests.cause_beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that chew young corn leaves. One kind also carries the germ that causes Stewart's wilt, a corn disease, spreading it as it feeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Seedlings usually outgrow light feeding; where beetles are thick, a floating row cover over young plants (removed at tasseling for pollination) protects them, and spinosad is labeled if needed.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Small plants usually grow past light damage. If the beetles are thick, cover the young plants with a lightweight row cover, taking it off when the tassels form so the wind can pollinate, and use an organic spinosad spray only if you must.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control weeds that harbor the beetles, plant after the soil warms so seedlings grow fast, and choose Stewart's-wilt-tolerant varieties where the disease occurs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull weeds that shelter the beetles, plant into warm soil so the corn grows quickly, and pick varieties that resist Stewart's wilt if it is a problem where you live.

pests.name: Raccoons
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ears pulled down, husked, and half-eaten overnight as the kernels fill, with stalks knocked flat; the damage can arrive fast once the ears are worth raiding.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ears torn open and eaten, and stalks knocked over, appearing overnight right when the corn is ready. Raccoons seem to know the exact night before you plan to harvest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Raccoons, which raid corn from the milk and dough stages on and can strip a patch in a night or two; they are one of the most common causes of a lost home crop.
pests.cause_beginner: Raccoons, which raid ripe corn at night and can clear a small patch in a night or two. They are one of the most common reasons a home corn crop is lost.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no spray; exclusion is the answer. A two-wire electric fence (about 4 and 8 inches high) turned on as ears near maturity is the most reliable home defense.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot spray for raccoons; you have to keep them out. A short two-wire electric fence, switched on as the ears get close to ready, is the surest way to protect the patch.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Put the fence up and energize it before the ears fill out, not after the first raid, since once raccoons find the patch they return nightly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Set up and turn on the fence before the corn is ripe, not after the first raid. Once raccoons find your corn, they come back every night.

diseases.name: Common smut
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery-white galls on ears, tassels, or stalks that swell, then rupture to release a mass of powdery black spores; ear galls replace kernels and are most common on stressed or injured plants.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Puffy silver-white growths on the ears or stalks that later burst into a cloud of black powder. On the ear, these galls take the place of kernels. They show up most on stressed or damaged plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Ustilago maydis, which enters through wounds and silks and is favored by hot, dry weather punctuated by injury; its spores survive years in the soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that gets in through wounds and silks, especially in hot, dry spells, and forms the galls. Its spores can survive in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no spray for the home garden; cut off and bag the galls before they rupture and blacken, to keep spores out of the soil. Do not compost them.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home spray. Cut off and throw away (do not compost) the galls before they burst, so their spores do not spread into your soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid wounding plants during cultivation, keep moisture and fertility steady to reduce stress, rotate away from infected beds, and choose more tolerant varieties where smut recurs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Try not to injure the plants while weeding, keep water and feeding steady so the corn is not stressed, move your corn each year, and pick more resistant varieties if smut keeps coming back.

diseases.name: Common rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small cinnamon-brown, powdery pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces, darkening toward the season's end; heavy infection yellows and kills leaf tissue and can cut ear fill.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small rusty-brown, powdery spots on both sides of the leaves that darken later in the season. A bad case yellows the leaves and can leave the ears less full.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Puccinia sorghi, whose spores blow in on the wind and infect under cool, moist, humid conditions; it does not overwinter in most northern gardens but arrives each year on wind currents.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus whose spores blow in on the wind and take hold in cool, damp weather. In most gardens it arrives fresh each year rather than surviving the winter in place.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Most home crops tolerate rust without treatment; remove badly infected lower leaves to slow spread and improve airflow. A labeled fungicide is rarely needed in a garden.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Most gardens can live with a little rust. Pull off the worst lower leaves to slow it and give the plants air. You rarely need to spray in a home garden.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose rust-resistant hybrids, which are widely available, and plant early so the crop matures before rust builds late in the season; avoid overhead watering where practical.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick rust-resistant varieties, which are easy to find, and plant early so the corn is nearly done before rust gets bad late in summer. Water at the base when you can.

diseases.name: Stewart's wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Long, pale-green to yellow streaks with wavy margins running along the leaves, following flea-beetle feeding scars; severe early infection wilts and stunts seedlings, sometimes killing them.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Long yellow streaks with wavy edges running down the leaves, appearing after flea beetles have been feeding. A bad early case wilts and stunts young plants and can kill them.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Pantoea stewartii, carried and introduced by the corn flea beetle; mild winters that let more beetles survive drive worse outbreaks the following year.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium spread by the corn flea beetle as it feeds. After a mild winter more beetles survive, so the disease tends to be worse the next year.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy severely affected seedlings. Management is aimed at the flea-beetle vector, not the bacterium itself.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant; pull and throw away badly affected seedlings. The real control is keeping the flea beetles that spread it in check.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Grow resistant or tolerant hybrids, the primary defense, and manage flea beetles on young plants with row cover or a labeled treatment to break the transmission cycle.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow resistant varieties, which is the main defense, and keep flea beetles off young plants with a row cover or an organic treatment so they cannot pass the disease along.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water regularly to keep the root zone evenly moist through the season, with the highest demand from tasseling through silking and ear fill.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist. Pay the closest attention from the time the tassels appear through when the ears are filling out, which is when corn needs water the most.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week from rain and irrigation, rising toward 1.5 inches per week across the pollination and ear-fill window; water deeply to wet the full root zone.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, and closer to 1.5 inches while the corn is pollinating and filling ears. Water deeply so it soaks down to the roots rather than just wetting the surface.
watering.method_seasoned: Deep soaking at intervals suits corn. Overhead watering is tolerated far better than on disease-prone crops, but soaker or furrow watering conserves water and keeps the canopy from staying wet.
watering.method_beginner: Give corn a deep soak rather than frequent light sprinkles. Corn handles overhead watering better than many crops, but watering at the base wastes less and keeps the leaves drier.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and stunted, stalled growth in ground that stays wet point to waterlogged, oxygen-starved roots.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the lower leaves yellow while the plant stalls, the roots are drowning. Ease off and let it drain.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Leaves that roll or curl at midday, especially near tasseling, signal drought stress; stress in the silking window desiccates silks and pollen and leaves gappy, poorly filled ears.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Leaves that roll up like tubes in the afternoon mean the corn is too dry. If this happens while the tassels and silks are out, you get ears with missing kernels, so keep the water steady then.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the seedbed evenly moist, never soggy
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Sown into warm soil, corn wants an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not saturated: cold, waterlogged soil rots the seed.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the seedbed evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Cold, wet soil rots the seed before it sprouts.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the top few inches evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grow young plants on with steady, even moisture while the root system establishes.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water the young plants evenly as they get their roots down.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 inch per week, wetting the full root zone
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Water use climbs steadily as the plants gain height; keep about 1 inch per week and water deeply to follow the deepening roots.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Give about 1 inch of water a week as the plants shoot up, and water deeply so it reaches the growing roots.

schedule_by_stage.rate: toward 1.5 inches per week, never let it dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Tasseling opens the critical-moisture window: water stress now, as pollen sheds, cuts pollen viability and the eventual kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: When the tassels are shedding pollen, the corn must not dry out. Dry soil now means poorly filled ears later, so keep the water steady and generous.

schedule_by_stage.rate: toward 1.5 inches per week, never let it dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Silking is the single most moisture-sensitive stage: drought desiccates the silks and drops pollination, giving blank tips and gappy ears. This is where steady water pays off most.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the plants get dry now, the silks cannot do their job and the ears come out with gaps, so water deeply and keep it up.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 1.5 inches per week
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Demand stays high as the kernels fill and harden; stress here aborts kernels at the ear tip. Hold steady moisture through the fill, then ease off as the crop nears maturity so the grain can begin to dry.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the kernels fill and harden, since letting it dry now costs you kernels at the tip. As the crop nears the end, ease off so the grain can start to dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: little to none; let the crop dry down
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Ease off and then stop watering as the crop nears maturity so the kernels can dry down on the stalk toward popping moisture. Popcorn is harvested dry and hard, not at a plump milk stage, so a dry finish is what you want.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Cut back and then stop watering as the corn nears the end, so the ears can dry out on the plant. Popcorn is picked dry and hard, not soft and juicy, so you want it to dry down at the finish.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The critical moisture window is tasseling through silking and into ear fill; do not let the bed dry out then.
watering.method_note_beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is when the tassels and silks are out and the ears are filling.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Tasseling, silking, and ear fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought at silking is the single most damaging, giving gappy, poorly filled ears.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Tasseling, silking, and ear-filling are when corn most needs steady water. Drying out during silking is the worst, and leaves ears with missing kernels.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Popcorn is direct-sown in place and is not started indoors or hardened off.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off corn. It is planted straight into the garden from seed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow into warm soil (at least 60°F) after the last spring frost. Corn resents root disturbance and germinates quickly in place, so transplanting offers little gain and risks setting plants back.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant corn seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F and frost is past. Corn does not like having its roots disturbed and comes up fast anyway, so there is little reason to start it indoors.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fully dried, shelled popcorn stores at room temperature in an airtight container. The trick with popcorn is to lock in its moisture at about 13 to 14 percent: a sealed jar keeps the kernels from drying out any further, since over-dry popcorn pops poorly or not at all. Keep the jars somewhere cool, dry, and dark.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Once the kernels are fully dry and shelled off the cob, popcorn keeps at room temperature in a sealed jar. Airtight storage matters, because it holds the kernels at the right moisture for popping. Kept sealed in a cool, dry spot, popcorn stays good for years.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigeration is not needed. Chilling or freezing the shelled kernels for a few days before storage is a simple way to kill any weevils or grain-moth eggs; return them to a sealed jar afterward so they neither pick up nor lose moisture.
storage.fridge_beginner: You do not need to refrigerate popcorn, but putting the shelled kernels in the fridge or freezer for a few days first is a good way to kill any tiny insects. Put them back in a sealed jar so they stay at the right dryness.
storage.freezer_seasoned: For long keeping, seal fully dried kernels airtight and freeze them; popcorn holds its popping quality for years this way. Let a jar come back to room temperature before you open it, so condensation does not wet the kernels.
storage.freezer_beginner: The freezer is a great place to keep popcorn for a long time in a sealed jar. Before you open a cold jar, let it warm up to room temperature first, so moisture from the air does not settle on the kernels.
storage.notes_seasoned: The whole storage task with popcorn is holding it at its popping moisture of about 13 to 14 percent. Unlike corn grown for meal, you are not trying to dry it as far as possible: too dry and it will not pop. Seal it airtight and it keeps its pop for years; a batch that has gone chewy or refuses to pop is telling you its moisture has drifted out of that window.
storage.notes_beginner: Storing popcorn is all about keeping it at the right dryness for popping, around 13 to 14 percent moisture. You are not trying to dry it out completely the way you would corn for cornmeal, because popcorn that is too dry will not pop. Keep it in a sealed jar and it stays good for years.

recommended.name: Tom Thumb
recommended.note: An early, dwarf popcorn for short seasons and small gardens. The plants stay low and the little ears dry down fast, so it finishes where a full-season type would not. A good pick for northern and cool-summer areas.

recommended.name: Robust R128YH
recommended.note: A dependable modern yellow hybrid with strong disease resistance and high popping expansion. This is the everyday snacking popcorn, a butterfly-flake type; grow it in a block and let the ears dry down before you test-pop and shell.

recommended.name: Gourmet Mushroom
recommended.note: A mushroom-type hybrid whose kernels pop into dense, round balls rather than winged flakes, so they hold caramel and coatings without shattering. Grown like any popcorn and cured to 13 to 14 percent moisture for the best pop.

recommended.name: Strawberry De-Lite
recommended.note: An ornamental strawberry popcorn with small, plump, deep-red strawberry-shaped ears that are as decorative as they are edible and still pop into small, tender flakes. Dry the little ears fully, then shell and test-pop.

varieties.note_seasoned: Popcorn choice splits by pop shape and use. Yellow butterfly hybrids like the Robust series are the dependable, high-popping workhorses; mushroom types (Gourmet Mushroom) pop into dense round balls that hold caramel and seasonings; the tender heirloom Japanese Hulless is prized for its nearly hull-free eating; and ornamentals like Strawberry and Dakota Black are grown as much for the jewel-colored ears as for a smaller but respectable pop. Short-season gardeners can reach for an early dwarf like Tom Thumb. Whatever you grow, isolate it from every other corn, sweet or field, since any stray pollen spoils the pop.
varieties.note_beginner: There are a few kinds to choose from. Reliable yellow hybrids like the Robust types are the easiest and highest-popping. Mushroom types pop into round balls that hold caramel well. The old heirloom Japanese Hulless is loved for its tender, almost hull-free popped corn, and colorful ornamentals like Strawberry (deep red) and Dakota Black (blue-black) are pretty enough to display and still pop. If your season is short, an early dwarf like Tom Thumb ripens fastest. Whichever you pick, keep it far from all other corn, because pollen from sweet or field corn will ruin its popping.

thinning.when: when seedlings are 3 to 4 inches tall
thinning.method: snip extra seedlings at the soil line
thinning.tip_seasoned: If you sow thickly to insure a stand, thin within the block to a final in-row spacing of 8 to 12 inches once seedlings are a few inches tall. Snip the extras at the soil line rather than pulling, to spare the shallow roots of the plants you keep.
thinning.tip_beginner: If you plant the seeds close together to be sure they come up, thin them to about 8 to 12 inches apart within the block when they are a few inches tall. Cut the extra seedlings off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not disturb the roots of the ones you are keeping.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Popcorn is not suited to pots. It grows tall, feeds heavily, and must be planted in a block of several plants for wind pollination, so it belongs in a garden bed, not a container.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Popcorn is a poor container crop: it is tall and hungry and depends on a block planting for wind pollination, none of which a single pot supports. Grow it in the ground.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following corn with corn in the same bed; rotating breaks the buildup of soil-borne diseases and corn pests, and spreads out the crop's heavy nitrogen demand.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Try not to plant corn in the same spot two years running. Moving it each year keeps corn diseases and pests from building up and gives the soil a rest from its heavy feeding.
rotation.good_after: Corn follows a legume well: beans or peas leave nitrogen in the soil that this hungry crop puts straight to use.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate corn on a two-to-three-year cycle and place it after a nitrogen-fixing legume where you can, since corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your corn to a new spot each year, on about a two-to-three-year cycle. Planting it where beans or peas grew the year before gives it the extra nitrogen it wants.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow about 1 to 2 inches deep once soil is at least 60°F, into a block of short rows; sow the small-kerneled types a little shallower. Keep the seedbed evenly moist but not saturated, since cold, wet soil rots the seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the seeds about 1 to 2 inches deep once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, laying out a block of short rows rather than one long row. Plant small-kerneled kinds a bit shallower. Keep the bed evenly damp but not soggy, because cold, wet soil rots the seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for roughly a week, then the coleoptile spikes through and the first blade unfurls. Emergence takes about 4 to 7 days in warm soil and much longer in cool soil.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a pointed shoot pushes up and the first leaf opens. Corn comes up in about 4 to 7 days in warm soil, slower when it is cool.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your corn seedlings emerged? Note the date to track real days from sowing rather than the seed-packet estimate.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your corn come up yet? Write down the date you first saw the seedlings break the soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the block evenly moist and weed-free; young corn competes poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly to spare the surface roots. Thin now to a final 8 to 12 inches in the row if you sowed thickly.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, since small corn does not compete well with them. Weed shallowly to protect the roots near the surface. If you planted thickly, thin to about 8 to 12 inches apart now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The seedlings put out a few strap-shaped leaves and stand a few inches tall by around two to three weeks. This is the stage flea beetles and cutworms do the most harm, so watch for pinholes and clipped stems.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The young plants send up several long, narrow leaves and reach a few inches tall by two or three weeks. This is when flea beetles and cutworms can do the most damage, so watch for tiny holes and cut-off stems.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your corn stand looking? Note any gaps, thinning you did, or early insect damage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young corn plants look? Note any bare patches, thinning, or chewed leaves.

growth_stages.name: Vegetative
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and keep moisture steady as the plants stretch up. Hill a little soil around the base for support, and hold off overhead work that could injure stalks and invite smut.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen when the plants are about knee-high, and keep the water steady as they shoot up. Pull a little soil around the bases to steady the tall stalks, and avoid injuring them, which can let in disease.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid upward growth from a few inches to knee-high and beyond, adding leaves and building the stalk that will carry the ears. Reproductive parts (tassel and ears) are being set inside now, so steady water and feeding here shape the crop.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fast upward growth from a few inches to knee-high and taller, adding leaves and thickening the stalk. Inside, the plant is already forming the tassel and ears, so steady water and feeding at this stage set up your harvest.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your corn filling in? Note the height, leaf count, and any sidedressing you did.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How tall is your corn getting? Note its height and when you fed it.

growth_stages.name: Tasseling
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out: this is the start of the critical-moisture window. Keep water high and steady, sidedress nitrogen again as tassels emerge, and avoid anything that knocks pollen off prematurely.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous now, because this begins the most important stretch for the crop. Feed once more with nitrogen as the tassels appear, and try not to shake the plants and lose pollen early.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The tassel pushes out of the top of the stalk and begins shedding pollen. This is one of the two most weather-sensitive stages: heat over 95°F or drought here kills pollen and thins the eventual kernel set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A feathery tassel appears at the very top of each stalk and starts releasing pollen. This is one of the two touchiest weather stages: hot spells over 95°F or dry soil now ruin the pollen and leave you with gappy ears.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have the tassels emerged? Note the date and any heat or dry spell during pollen shed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have the tassels come out at the top? Note the date and whether it was hot or dry while they shed pollen.

growth_stages.name: Silking
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold moisture at its peak: silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage. Water deeply through any heat wave, and do not disturb the block while pollen is shedding onto the fresh silks.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water at its highest and steadiest now, because silking is the stage that suffers most from dry soil. Water deeply through any hot spell, and leave the plants alone while pollen is landing on the fresh silks.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Silks emerge from the ear tips a couple of days after the tassel opens; each silk that catches pollen becomes one kernel. Silks stay receptive for up to two weeks. Brown, dry silks with no pollination leave blank ears.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Silks come out of the top of each young ear a day or two after the tassels open, and every silk that catches pollen turns into one kernel. The silks can be pollinated for up to two weeks. Silks that dry up without pollen mean empty ears.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have the silks emerged? Note the date the first silks showed, to time the harvest about 18 to 20 days later.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have the silks appeared at the top of the ears? Note the date, since the corn is usually ready about 18 to 20 days after.

growth_stages.name: Kernel Fill
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady as the kernels fill and harden; stress now aborts tip kernels. Then ease off water as the crop nears maturity so the grain can begin to dry. Leave the ears on the stalk to finish.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the kernels fill out and harden, since drying out now costs you kernels at the tip. As the crop nears the end, let it dry out a little so the grain can start to harden. Leave the ears on the plant.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The ears reach full size and the kernels pass from milky through a stiff dough to a hard, glassy flint. Popcorn kernels stay small and dense rather than plumping like sweet corn; the husks stay green for now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The ears reach full size and the kernels change from soft and milky to a firm dough and then to hard and glossy. Popcorn kernels stay small and dense rather than swelling up like sweet corn. The husks are still green at this point.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the kernels hardening? Note when they passed the dough stage and turned glassy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are the kernels getting hard and glossy? Note when they firmed up.

growth_stages.name: Dry-Down
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering and let the crop dry on the stalk. Little needs doing now except protecting the ears from birds and raccoons and, in humid regions, watching for mold on any ears with loose or damaged husks. The longer the kernels dry on the plant in good weather, the closer they get to popping moisture.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering and let the corn dry out on the plant. There is little to do now except keep birds and raccoons off the ears and, if your weather is humid, watch for any ears whose husks are loose or split, since those can mold. The more the kernels dry on the stalk in good weather, the better.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant yellows and dies back, the husks turn from green to brown and papery, and the kernels harden and lose moisture. A black layer forms at the base of each kernel at physiological maturity, after which no more starch is added and the grain simply dries toward the popping window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The whole plant turns brown and dies back, the husks go from green to dry and papery, and the kernels get hard and glossy. After the kernels are fully formed they just keep drying out on the plant, heading toward the moisture that lets them pop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have the husks browned and the kernels hardened? Note the date the crop reached the hard, glassy, drying-down stage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have the husks dried brown and the kernels gone hard and glossy? Note the date the corn started drying down.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick the ears once the husks are brown and papery and the kernels are hard and glossy. In dry weather you can leave them longer on the stalk to field-dry; in humid weather, pull them at hard-dry to beat mold. There is no narrow window, so harvest at your convenience once the kernels are hard, then finish drying under cover.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the ears when the husks have turned brown and papery and the kernels are hard and glossy. If the weather is dry you can leave them on the stalk to dry further; if it is humid, pick them so they do not mold. There is no rush, so harvest whenever it suits you once the kernels are hard, then finish drying them indoors.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Brown, papery husks, dead silks, and hard, glassy kernels that barely mark under a thumbnail. Unlike milk-stage sweet corn, the ear is meant to be fully mature and dry, not plump and green.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Brown, papery husks, dead silks, and hard, glossy kernels that do not dent when you press them with a thumbnail. Unlike sweet corn, you want the ear fully mature and dry, not green and juicy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you brought in the dried ears? Log the harvest date and roughly how many ears the block gave.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked the dried ears? Note the date and about how many ears you got.

growth_stages.name: Cure and Shell
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Shuck the harvested ears, put them in mesh bags, and hang them in a warm, dry, airy place for two to three weeks to finish drying. Once or twice a week, shell a few kernels and test-pop them: when they pop up crisp and fluffy, shell the whole ear and store the kernels. Stop drying at the popping window (about 13 to 14 percent moisture); take the ears no further, since over-dry kernels will not pop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pull the husks back, put the ears in mesh bags, and hang them somewhere warm, dry, and airy for two to three weeks. Once or twice a week, twist off a few kernels and try popping them. When they pop up crisp and fluffy, they are ready, so shell the ears and store the kernels. Do not over-dry them, because popcorn that is too dry will not pop.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Kernels that shell cleanly off the cob and pop up crisp, fluffy, and fully expanded in the test batch. Chewy or jagged pops mean the kernels are still too wet and need more time; a sample that fails to pop means they have dried past the window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Kernels that come off the cob easily and pop up crisp and fluffy when you test them. If they come out chewy or jagged, they are still too wet and need to dry more. If they will not pop at all, they got too dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you test-popped and stored the kernels? Note the date and how the sample popped.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you tested a batch and stored the kernels? Note the date and how well they popped.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow popcorn after the last spring frost, once the soil is at least 60°F. Plant a BLOCK of at least four short rows, 1 to 2 inches deep, for good wind pollination. Keep it isolated from sweet corn and field corn, whose pollen keeps popcorn from popping.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant popcorn right in the garden after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant a block of at least four short rows, 1 to 2 inches deep, so the wind can pollinate it. Keep it well away from sweet corn and field corn.

notifications.body_seasoned: Tasseling and silking are the critical-moisture window. Water deeply and keep the bed evenly moist; drought or heat over 95°F now gives gappy, poorly filled ears.
notifications.body_beginner: Your corn is tasseling and silking, which is when it needs water the most. Keep the soil evenly moist and water deeply. Dry soil or heat over 95°F now leaves ears with missing kernels.

notifications.title_beginner: Let your popcorn dry on the stalk
notifications.body_seasoned: Popcorn is left to mature and dry on the stalk. Watch for the husks to turn brown and papery and the kernels to harden to a glassy flint, then pick and finish drying under cover before test-popping. There is no narrow window.
notifications.body_beginner: Popcorn is left to dry out on the plant. Wait for the husks to turn brown and papery and the kernels to get hard and glossy, then pick the ears and finish drying them indoors. There is no rush.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming, protect young corn
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Popcorn is frost-tender while it is green and growing. If frost is forecast, cover young plants with row cover overnight. Once the kernels have hardened, a frost simply ends the season and the mature ears can still be dried.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Popcorn is killed by frost while it is still green and growing, so cover young plants with row cover if frost is forecast. Once the kernels are hard and glossy, a frost just ends the season, and you can still dry the mature ears.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat over 95°F during tasseling and silking depresses pollen production and desiccates silks, cutting the kernel set. Water deeply ahead of and through the heat to buffer the plants.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Heat over 95°F while the corn is tasseling and silking damages the pollen and dries out the silks, so the ears do not fill. Water deeply before and during the hot spell to help the plants through it.

germination.text_seasoned: Plant corn in a BLOCK, not a long single row. Corn is wind-pollinated: the tassel sheds pollen that must fall on the silks, and a block of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid) fills the ears far better than one long row where pollen blows off to the side.
germination.text_beginner: Plant corn in a square block of short rows, not one long row. Corn is pollinated by wind, so the pollen from the tassels has to drift down onto the silks. A block of at least four short rows (think four rows of four) keeps the pollen among the plants, so the ears fill out with full kernels.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Wait for soil at least 60°F before sowing. Corn seed rots or takes chilling injury in cold, wet ground, and there is no head start to be had from early planting.
germination.text_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting. Corn seed rots in cold, wet soil, so planting early just gives you gaps in the stand. There is nothing to gain by rushing.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Keep popcorn away from sweet corn AND field corn: pollen from either one crossing onto your popcorn keeps the kernels from popping. Isolate by at least 300 feet, or, since that is impractical in most home gardens, stagger tasseling by at least two weeks.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep popcorn away from sweet corn and field corn. Pollen from either will drift in and ruin its popping. Keep them at least 300 feet apart, or, since that is a lot of room, plant them so they tassel about two weeks apart instead.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and again as tassels form. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and the two demand peaks are rapid stalk growth and the run-up to pollination; sandy soils call for splitting it further.
vegetative.text_beginner: Feed corn with nitrogen when it is about knee-high and again when the tassels appear. Corn is a hungry crop, and those are the two times it needs the most food. In sandy soil, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
vegetative.author: plant

tasseling.text_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out at tasseling. Heat over 95°F or drought as pollen sheds kills pollen viability and thins the kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady through the pollination window.
tasseling.text_beginner: Keep the soil moist while the tassels are shedding pollen. Hot weather over 95°F or dry soil now ruins the pollen, so the ears end up with missing kernels. Water deeply and keep it steady through this stretch.
tasseling.author: plant

silking.text_seasoned: Silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage: stress here desiccates silks and pollen and gives the greatest yield loss of any timing. Water deeply through any heat wave while the silks are receptive.
silking.text_beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the corn dries out now, the silks cannot catch and hold pollen, and that costs you more than dry weather at any other time. Water deeply through any hot spell while the silks are out.
silking.author: plant

kernel_fill.text_seasoned: Hold steady moisture through ear fill, then ease off as the crop nears maturity. Once pollination has succeeded, dry conditions show up as aborted kernels at the ear tip, so keep water even until the kernels are well filled.
kernel_fill.text_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the ears fill, then ease off as the corn nears the end. After the corn has been pollinated, dry soil shows up as missing kernels at the tip of the ear, so do not let it dry out until the kernels are full.
kernel_fill.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest popcorn dry, not green. Let the husks turn brown and papery and the kernels harden to a glassy flint, then pick and finish drying under cover before test-popping and shelling. Unlike sweet corn there is no 4-to-5-day window, so the timing is forgiving.
harvest.text_beginner: Harvest popcorn dry, not green like sweet corn. Wait until the husks are brown and papery and the kernels are hard and glossy, then pick the ears and finish drying them indoors before you test-pop and shell. There is no narrow window to catch, so the timing is easy.
harvest.author: plant

dry_down.text_seasoned: Let popcorn dry down on the stalk and stop watering once the kernels harden. In dry weather leave the ears standing to field-dry toward popping moisture; in humid weather watch for mold and be ready to pick at hard-dry and finish under cover.
dry_down.text_beginner: Let popcorn dry out on the plant and stop watering once the kernels are hard. In dry weather you can leave the ears standing to keep drying on the stalk. In humid weather, watch for mold and be ready to pick them and finish drying them indoors.
dry_down.author: plant

cure_thresh.text_seasoned: After picking, shuck the ears, bag them in mesh, and hang them in a warm, dry, airy place for two to three weeks. Test-pop a few kernels once or twice a week; when they pop crisp and fluffy, shell and store. Stop at the popping window of about 13 to 14 percent moisture, since over-dry kernels will not pop.
cure_thresh.text_beginner: After you pick the ears, pull the husks back, put them in mesh bags, and hang them somewhere warm, dry, and airy for two to three weeks. Test-pop a few kernels each week, and once they pop up crisp and fluffy, shell and store them. Do not over-dry them, or they will stop popping.
cure_thresh.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Each stalk yields one to two mature ears of popcorn, and the small-kerneled dwarf types can set several little ears per plant. Home plantings are measured in ears rather than bushels: a 10-foot block row returns roughly a dozen to two dozen dried ears, which shell out to a few pounds of kernels for popping.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives about one or two ears, and the small dwarf types can set several little ears each. A 10-foot row in your block yields roughly a dozen to two dozen dried ears, which comes to a few pounds of kernels once you shell them off the cobs.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Unlike sweet corn there is no fleeting peak. The whole block matures and dries down together over a few weeks in fall, and the dry kernels then keep for years, so the harvest is a single event rather than a race against the milk stage.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: There is no rush like there is with sweet corn. The whole block dries down together in fall, you bring it in once, and the dry kernels keep for years, so you harvest it all at once instead of checking it every day.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Popcorn is easy to grow but demands space, a long season, and patience: it needs a block of several rows for pollination and a full 90 to 110 days to dry down, plus a couple of weeks of curing to reach the popping moisture. Its great advantage over sweet corn is a forgiving, one-shot harvest and kernels that store for years.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Popcorn is not hard to grow, but it needs room and time: a block of several rows and a long, warm season of 90 to 110 days to dry down, then a couple more weeks of drying to get it popping right. The payoff is an easy harvest with no daily checking, and kernels that store for years.
factors_seasoned: Block planting for wind pollination (a single row or a few plants pollinates poorly and gives gappy ears)
Strict isolation from all other corn (sweet or dent pollen crossing onto popcorn keeps it from popping)
Steady moisture at tasseling and silking (the critical window; drought here is the largest yield loss)
A long enough frost-free season to reach dry-down (90 to 110 days; the limiting factor in short-season regions)
Curing to the popping window (about 13 to 14 percent moisture; too wet pops poorly, too dry will not pop)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing popcorn planting by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature (at least 60°F) and your frost-free date, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Ears with gaps and missing kernels
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Ears with bare patches and missing kernels
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ears filled unevenly with blank patches because pollination failed on those silks. The usual causes are a too-small planting (a single row or a few plants), heat over 95°F or drought during silking that killed pollen and dried the silks, or silks that were never dusted because the block was too sparse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The ears came out with bare patches because those silks never got pollinated. This usually happens when the corn was planted in too small a group (a single row or a few plants), or when heat or dry soil during silking ruined the pollen and dried up the silks.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant a BLOCK of at least four short rows so wind pollination is thorough, and keep moisture high and steady through tasseling and silking. Time plantings so silking misses the worst summer heat, and hand-shake the tassels at midday in a small planting to help.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a block of at least four short rows so the wind can pollinate well, and keep the water steady while the tassels and silks are out. Try to time it so silking is not in the hottest part of summer, and in a small patch you can gently shake the tassels at midday to spread pollen.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seed rotted or came up in a thin, patchy stand
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or came up thin and patchy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The seed was sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so it sat and rotted or suffered chilling injury in the first day or two after sowing instead of germinating.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seed went into soil that was too cold and wet, so it rotted or was damaged by the cold in the first day or two instead of sprouting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until soil is at least 60°F at sowing depth; there is no benefit to early sowing. Plant into warm, well-drained ground rather than a cold, wet spot, and do not over-water the seedbed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, since planting early only rots the seed. Plant into warm, well-drained soil instead of a cold, wet spot, and do not keep the seedbed soggy.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ears were pulled down, husked, and eaten and stalks knocked flat as the kernels filled. Raccoons (and sometimes deer or birds) raid corn from the milk and dough stages on and can strip a small patch in a night or two.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The ears were torn open and eaten and the stalks knocked over as the corn filled out. Raccoons (and sometimes deer or birds) raid corn once the kernels start to fill and can clear a small patch in a night or two.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Exclusion is the reliable defense: put up a two-wire electric fence (about 4 and 8 inches high) and energize it BEFORE the ears fill out, since once raccoons find the patch they return nightly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: The sure fix is to keep them out. Set up a short two-wire electric fence and turn it on before the ears fill out, not after the first raid, because once raccoons find your corn they come back every night.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ears grew and dried, but the shelled kernels pop poorly or not at all. There are two usual causes. First, moisture: kernels still too wet pop small and chewy, while kernels dried past the popping window (about 13 to 14 percent) fail to pop at all. Second, cross-pollination: if sweet corn or field corn pollinated the popcorn, the resulting kernels have altered endosperm and will not pop no matter how they are dried.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The ears grew and dried fine, but the kernels pop badly or not at all. Usually it is one of two things. Either the moisture is wrong, kernels that are too wet pop small and chewy and kernels that got too dry will not pop, or the popcorn was cross-pollinated by nearby sweet corn or field corn, which stops it from popping no matter how you dry it.
failure_diagnostics.cause: wrong kernel moisture or cross-pollination by other corn
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cure to the popping window and test-pop before storing: dry to about 13 to 14 percent, and stop there rather than over-drying. And isolate the popcorn from every other corn, by at least 300 feet or by staggering tasseling about two weeks, so no sweet or dent pollen reaches the ears.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Dry the kernels to the right point and test-pop a batch before storing the crop, and do not over-dry them. Just as important, keep popcorn well away from all other corn next year, at least 300 feet apart or planted to tassel about two weeks apart, so its pollen is not spoiled.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Ears molded or never dried down
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Ears molded or would not dry
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ears failed to dry to popping moisture, or grew mold on the cob, because the crop ran into cool, wet, humid fall weather or a killing frost before it finished drying down. Field-drying stalls in persistent damp, and ears left out in the wet mold rather than curing.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The ears did not dry out properly, or grew moldy, because cool, wet, humid fall weather or an early frost caught the crop before it finished drying. Corn barely dries in cold, damp weather, and ears left out in the wet tend to mold instead of curing.
failure_diagnostics.cause: season too short or too humid for field drying
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose an earlier variety matched to your season, sow as early as warm soil allows so the crop dries down with margin before fall, and in humid regions pick the ears at hard-dry and finish drying them indoors in mesh bags with airflow rather than leaving them out in the wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick an earlier variety that fits your season and sow as soon as the soil is warm, so the corn dries down with time to spare before fall. In humid areas, bring the ears in and finish drying them indoors in mesh bags with a fan instead of leaving them out in damp weather.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Popcorn is a single full-season crop, not a succession crop. You sow once after the last spring frost and grow the whole block to a dry-down harvest in fall, so there is no staggered replanting. Give it the longest run of frost-free weather you have, since a late sowing may not dry down before frost.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant popcorn once and grow it the whole season, so there is no need to replant every couple of weeks. Sow after the last frost and give it plenty of time, because it needs a long, warm season to dry down before fall.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Hawaii has no real winter, so you can sow popcorn year-round in the lowlands. The catch is the humid tropical air, which dries kernels slowly, so plan to finish drying the ears indoors.
